Eucharistic Adoration
yoo-kuh-RIS-tik ad-oh-RAY-shun
noun phrase (a Roman practice)
From “Eucharist” (Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving) and “adoration”; the Roman practice of worshipping the consecrated host as the body of Christ, resting on transubstantiation.

📖 Biblical Definition

Eucharistic adoration is the Roman Catholic practice of worshipping the consecrated host—the bread of the Mass—as the very body of Christ, bowing before it, exposing it in the monstrance, and adoring it as God. It rests upon the dogma of transubstantiation, that at the priest's words the substance of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ while the appearances remain. The dictionary rejects both the dogma and the adoration as grave corruptions of the Lord's Supper and as idolatry. The Lord instituted the Supper as a memorial and a sign-and-seal: “This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.” He spoke figuratively, as He did when He called Himself the door and the vine; the bread signifies and seals His body, but is not changed into it. To bow down before bread as God is to worship the creature and to break the second commandment, which forbids the making and adoring of any image or object as the deity. Moreover, God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth, not in a wafer. The dictionary further holds that the Supper is no repeated sacrifice, for Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever and by one offering hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified; the Mass, claiming to re-present that sacrifice, dishonours its finished sufficiency. The Reformed believer feeds upon Christ by faith, receiving Him spiritually present to the soul, and adores Christ enthroned in heaven—never the bread upon the table.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Roman practice of worshipping the consecrated host as the body of Christ, resting on transubstantiation; rejected as idolatry and a corruption of the Supper, which is a memorial sign (Luke 22:19), not a wafer to be adored or a sacrifice re-offered.

EUCHARISTIC ADORATION, noun phrase. The Roman worship of the consecrated host as the body of Christ.

Rests on transubstantiation, the supposed change of bread into Christ's body.

The Supper is a memorial sign: “this do in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

To adore bread as God breaks the second commandment (Exodus 20:4).

Christ offered one sacrifice for ever (Hebrews 10:14); the Mass dishonours its sufficiency.

📖 Key Scripture

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Heb 10:14 — "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

Lu 22:19 — "And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me."

Ex 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Eucharistic adoration is itself the corruption: it worships bread as God on the false dogma of transubstantiation, breaking the second commandment and dishonouring the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.

expand to see more

Eucharistic adoration is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. Resting on transubstantiation, it bids men bow before a wafer and adore it as the living God. The dictionary names this idolatry. The Lord's words “this is my body” are figurative, as when He called Himself the vine and the door; the bread remains bread, a sign and seal of His body given. To worship the creature—here, bread—as the Creator is the very sin the second commandment forbids, and no priestly formula can turn an act of idolatry into worship in spirit and in truth.

The adoration is bound up with the further error of the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, re-presenting Christ's offering again and again. But Scripture is emphatic: Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, and by that one offering hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. To repeat or re-present that sacrifice is to deny its finished sufficiency. The dictionary holds the Reformed doctrine of the Supper: a memorial and a sign-and-seal, in which the believer by faith feeds spiritually upon the Christ who is bodily in heaven, and adores Him there—not in the bread, which he receives in remembrance, but never worships.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek eucharistia (thanksgiving) and the Latin adoratio (worship); the practice depends on the dogma of transubstantiatio, the supposed change of substance.

expand to see more

Eucharistia, Greek, “thanksgiving,” a name for the Lord's Supper from Christ's giving of thanks.

Adoratio, Latin, worship, here directed wrongly to the consecrated host.

Transubstantiatio, the supposed change of bread's substance into Christ's body.

“Monstrance,” the vessel in which the host is exposed for adoration.

Set against the second commandment and the once-for-all offering of Christ.

Usage

"The teacher named eucharistic adoration as idolatry, the worship of bread on the false dogma of transubstantiation."

"He held the Supper to be a memorial sign, not a wafer to be adored."

"She adored Christ enthroned in heaven, feeding on Him by faith, never bowing to the bread."
